etymology.text: From Middle High German geburttac, from Old High German giburtitag; equivalent to Geburt (“birth”) + -s- + Tag (“day”).

funFacts: Greece celebrates the name day (γιορτή) as much as the birthday; in Germany the birthday is the big day, the name day matters only in some Catholic regions.
pitfalls: German says Ich habe Geburtstag (I have birthday – no article): Ich habe im Mai Geburtstag.
Do not wish happy birthday before the day: many Germans think it brings bad luck (vorher gratulieren).
subtleties: The joining -s- (Geburt-s-tag) is a Fugen-s, common in German compounds.

contrasts.value: one’s own time off work, a trip

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Time off work: the beach, the mountains, the suitcase by the door.

examples.text: Im August haben wir Urlaub.
examples.tr: We’re on holiday in August.

examples.text: Wir fahren im Sommer in Urlaub.
examples.tr: We go on holiday in summer.

examples.text: Wie war dein Urlaub?
examples.tr: How was your holiday?

synonyms.nuance: holidays of a school, a university or an institution – plural only; in Switzerland also one’s own vacation
trip, journey – the travelling, not the time off

etymology.text: From Middle High German urloup. Related to erlauben (“to allow”). Cognate with English leave (“time off, permission to be away”).

funFacts: Urlaub was “permission to leave” – the English leave in “annual leave” is the same word, from the root of erlauben (to allow).
pitfalls: Urlaub is the time off from your job (Ich habe zwei Wochen Urlaub); school and university breaks are Ferien (plural only).
A public holiday (Christmas Day, 1 May) is ein Feiertag – neither Urlaub nor Ferien.
subtleties: in Urlaub fahren and in den Urlaub fahren are both correct.
Urlaub nehmen = to take days off (from the employer).

contrasts.value: school, university or parliament holidays (plural only)

plurals.none: plural only: the word itself is a plural (die Ferien)

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: No school! – the long summer break, the autumn and Easter holidays.

senses.def: holidays (of a school, university, parliament – plural only)
vacation, holiday (one’s own; especially in Switzerland and Austria)

examples.text: Im Sommer haben die Kinder sechs Wochen Ferien.
examples.tr: In summer the children have six weeks’ holiday.

examples.text: In den Ferien fahren wir zu Oma.
examples.tr: In the holidays we go to Grandma’s.

examples.text: Schöne Ferien!
examples.tr: Have a nice holiday!

examples.text: Wir gehen im Juli in die Ferien.
examples.tr: We’re going on holiday in July.

synonyms.nuance: holiday from work – your own time off as an employee

etymology.text: 15th century, from Latin fēriae (“holidays, feast days”), with the Latin plural ending -ae replaced by German -en.

funFacts: Latin feriae (festival days) also gave English fair (a market) and Spanish feria.
pitfalls: Ferien has no singular: die Ferien sind …, in den Ferien – never *eine Ferie.
Ferien = school / university / institutional breaks; Urlaub = time off your job.
subtleties: Each German state has its own school holiday dates, so the summer holidays are staggered across the country.

governs.when: mostly with no article (bis Montag, bis Berlin); before an article another preposition decides the case: bis zum Bahnhof

contractions.none: no merged forms with the article

profile.feeling: An end point – until Monday, see you tomorrow, as far as the station.

senses.def: until, till (time: bis Montag, bis acht Uhr)
to, as far as (place: bis Berlin, bis zum Bahnhof)

examples.text: Ich bleibe bis Sonntag.
examples.tr: I’m staying until Sunday.

examples.text: Bis morgen!
examples.tr: See you tomorrow!

examples.text: Das Geschäft ist von neun bis achtzehn Uhr offen.
examples.tr: The shop is open from nine to six.

examples.text: Der Bericht muss bis Freitag fertig sein.
examples.tr: The report must be finished by Friday.

examples.text: Der Bus fährt bis zum Bahnhof.
examples.tr: The bus goes as far as the station.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German biz, bit, bitze, from bī (“by”) + ze (“to”). Equivalent to modern bei and zu.

funFacts: bis is bei + zu fused – literally “by-to”, a point you go up to.
pitfalls: bis alone before words without an article (bis Montag, bis morgen, bis acht Uhr, bis Berlin); with an article add zu: bis zum Abend, bis zur Post.
bis is “until” and also “by” (a deadline): Ich bin bis Montag hier (until) – Bis Montag ist es fertig (by).
subtleties: bis is also a conjunction: Warte, bis ich komme. (Wait until I come.)
Goodbyes name the next meeting: bis später, bis bald, bis morgen, bis Montag.

contractions.none: no merged forms with the article

profile.feeling: Something that started in the past and is still going on.

senses.def: since (a point in time: seit Montag)
for (a period still going on: seit zwei Jahren)

examples.text: Ich bin seit Montag in Berlin.
examples.tr: I’ve been in Berlin since Monday.

examples.text: Wir warten seit zwanzig Minuten.
examples.tr: We’ve been waiting for twenty minutes.

examples.text: Sie lernt seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
examples.tr: She has been learning German for a year.

examples.text: Seit wann wohnst du hier?
examples.tr: How long have you been living here?

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German sīt, from Old High German sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīþuz. Akin to Old English sīþ. Related to Dutch sedert and sinds.

funFacts: Greek and Russian use the present here too: Μένω εδώ από το 2020 / Я живу здесь два года – German works the same way; English is the odd one out with “have been living”.
pitfalls: seit + PRESENT tense for something still going on: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier (not *habe … gewohnt, as English “have lived”).
seit always takes the dative: seit einem Jahr, seit zwei Wochen (Wochen = dative plural), seit dem Sommer.
seit (since / for, still going on) ≠ vor (ago): vor zwei Jahren = two years ago.
subtleties: Seit wann …? (since when) and Wie lange schon …? both ask how long something has been going on.
seit is also a conjunction: seit ich hier wohne … (since I have been living here).

contrasts.value: a period or an event, + genitive (während des Urlaubs)

governs.when: in everyday speech also the dative: während dem Essen

profile.feeling: Something happening inside a span of time – during the film, during the holidays.

examples.text: Während der Woche arbeite ich viel.
examples.tr: During the week I work a lot.

examples.text: Während des Films ist das Handy aus.
examples.tr: During the film the phone is off.

examples.text: Während der Ferien fahren wir ans Meer.
examples.tr: During the holidays we go to the seaside.

examples.text: Während ich koche, deckst du den Tisch.
examples.tr: While I cook, you lay the table.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From the present participle of währen (“to last, persist”), with rebracketing of währendes [noun], währender [noun] as während des [noun], während der [noun].

funFacts: während is a frozen participle: “lasting” (währen = to last) – während des Krieges was once “the war lasting”.
pitfalls: während takes the genitive in standard German: während des Urlaubs (masc./neut.: des + -s), während der Woche (fem.), während der Ferien (plural).
In everyday speech you will also hear the dative (während dem Essen) – avoid it in writing.
subtleties: während is also a conjunction: Während ich koche, liest er. (While I cook, he reads.) – and it can mean “whereas”.

profile.feeling: A point on the clock – at eight, at midnight.

senses.def: at (a clock time: um acht Uhr)
around (um den Tisch, um die Ecke)
about (es geht um …: it is about …)
by (a difference: um zehn Euro billiger)
um … zu: in order to (Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Berlin zu arbeiten)

examples.text: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr.
examples.tr: The train leaves at eight o’clock.

examples.text: Um wie viel Uhr beginnt der Film?
examples.tr: At what time does the film start?

examples.text: Wir sitzen um den Tisch.
examples.tr: We’re sitting around the table.

examples.text: Es geht um meine Familie.
examples.tr: It’s about my family.

examples.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Berlin zu arbeiten.
examples.tr: I am learning German in order to work in Berlin.

examples.text: Er spart Geld, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
examples.tr: He is saving money to buy a car.

examples.text: In dem Film geht es um eine Familie in Berlin.
examples.tr: The film is about a family in Berlin.

examples.text: Die Preise sind um zehn Prozent gestiegen.
examples.tr: Prices have risen by ten per cent.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German umbe, ümbe, from Old High German umbi, from Proto-West Germanic *umbi. Cognate with Dutch om.

funFacts: um is a cousin of Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “around”, as in amphitheatre) and Latin ambi-.
pitfalls: um is only for clock times: um acht Uhr – but am Montag (days), im Mai (months), in der Nacht.
Approximately = gegen or um … herum: gegen acht Uhr (around eight).
subtleties: um takes the accusative: um den Tisch, um die Ecke.
um … zu + infinitive = in order to (a later step).
